title: The knight: the piece that jumps
outcomes: Taps every square a knight can jump to, including captures
Knows the knight is not blocked by pieces in between, unlike rooks and bishops
Says why a knight in the corner has fewer choices than one in the centre

steps.text: That was a **knight**, the piece shaped like a horse's head. It jumps in an **L**: two squares along a file or a rank, then one square to the side. It is the only piece that jumps over others, so only its landing square matters, and that square must not hold one of your own pieces.

steps.caption: From d4 there are eight landing squares: two out, one across. The squares in between are never touched.

claims.statement: These are exactly the squares the knight on d4 can jump to.

steps.caption: At the start every piece is walled in by pawns, and the knights still get out. Both knights can jump out on move one, before any pawn has moved.

line.say: White's knight jumps over the pawns and lands on c3, with no pawn moved first.
Black's knight does the same, from g8 to f6.

claims.statement: From the start position the knight on b1 can jump only to these squares.

steps.caption: The landing square decides. Own pawns on c2 and e2 block those two jumps. The black pawns on b5 and f5 and the bishop on e6 can be captured by landing on them.

claims.statement: With white pawns on c2 and e2, the knight reaches these squares and no others.

steps.caption: In the corner six of the eight jumps would land off the board, so only b3 and c2 are left. On d4 none were lost. On an empty board a knight in the centre has more squares to choose from.

claims.statement: From a1 the knight can jump only to these squares.

steps.prompt: Say it back: how does a knight move, what is different about it compared with a rook or a bishop, and why does a knight in the corner have fewer jumps than one in the middle?

steps.text: **Compare.** A knight jumps in an L: two squares one way and one to the side. It jumps over any piece in between, so only the landing square matters. It cannot land on its own piece, but it can capture an enemy piece there.
